newsitem.title: USA: Dow ends firm but off highs as tech rally fumbles.
newsitem.headline: Dow ends firm but off highs as tech rally fumbles.

text.p: U.S. blue chips extended their recovery from Friday's sell-off but the upward momentum was tempered as a rally in the high-technology sector fumbled in the afternoon.

"It's like (Fed chief Alan) Greenspan never said what he said. The spin on that is: It's one thing to use rhetoric and another to use policy. He's not going to bring the economy down by trying to stop IBM from going higher. It was a shot across the bow," said Prudential Securities' Larry Wachtel.
After surging 82 points Monday, the Dow rose nine to 6473.

The Dow surged nearly 50 points earlier as investors snapped up chips and semiconductor-related issues on an upbeat book-to-bill report. The November book-to-bill ratio rose to 1.15 from 1.11 in October. A flat to slightly higher reading was seen. The ratio means manufacturers received $115 in new orders last month for every $100 in shipments.
But the tech rally later waned on profit-taking. After hitting a record intra-day high of 1328.36, the tech-laden Nasdaq Composite lost four to about 1313.
Chip heavyweight Intel lost one to 129-1/8, Micron fell 1-1/8 to 34 and Cypress Semiconductor was off 1/8 to 15-3/8.

"When you think of Intel as an example, it's gone to enormous heights. Intel has gone up 60 since its July bottom. The group has had enormous gains. Sell on the news. It's classic. I would be amazed if they used (the book to bill) as a platform for another move upward," Wachtel said.

Charlie Crane, director of research at Spears Benzak Salomon and Farrell, said, "The tech sector is going to be volatile to the nth degree over the next several weeks. Many stocks have been riding the coat tails of stocks like IBM and Intel, some with less justification than others. Many will deliver satisfactory earnings."
Analysts said investors were shrugging off cautionary comments made by Greenspan last Thursday that sent stocks reeling on Friday.

Among special situations, Black & Decker slumped 6-1/4 to 31-3/8 after forecasting fourth-quarter and 1996 results will fall below expectations. It also warned 1997 first-quarter earnings will fall below the year ago's. Salomon cut the stock.

Dow component Philip Morris rose 2-5/8 to 116-7/8 after hitting a year-high of 118. Analysts cited continued buying momentum after Goldman Sachs on Monday raised its 12-month price target to $135 from $125. Philip Morris rose 4-3/4 on Monday.
The company forecast fourth-quarter results will fall below analyst projections.
Standard Commercial surged 4-3/4 to 18-3/4. Wheat First Butcher Singer reiterated its buy rating and added the stock to the firm's action list.
The long bond lost 12/32 to yield 6.49 percent.
Wall Street still faces several key economic indicators this week, including November producer prices on Wednesday and consumer prices and retail sales on Thursday.
Komag slumped 5-7/8 to 27-1/4 after warning fourth-quarter results will fall below expectations. PaineWebber downgraded the supplier of thin-film media for computer hard disk drives.
Bay Networks lost 1-3/8 to 23-1/4. Bay's new CEO forecast earnings will be flat or near flat until Bay addresses issues including ineffective marketing and a lack of focus.
Stone Energy surged 2-1/4 to 25-7/8 after news it expects to test "a significant discovery well" drilled in a field in federal waters offshore Louisiana.
EXCEL Communications lost 4-3/4 to 23-1/4. Donaldson, Lufkin & Jenrette reduced its rating on Excel to market perform from buy.
Winners beat losers 13-11 on very heavy NYSE volume of 446 million shares.
The Nasdaq Composite fell 3.72 to 1312.55.
The S&P 500 fell 2.22 to 747.54.
(Figures official as of 1645 EST/2145 GMT).
-- Wall Street Desk 212-859-1721
